data_presentation.notes: Numbers are precise and consistently rounded: 16.6%, 9.1% sedan median, 13.1%, 24.3%, r=0.50, 39.9%->55.0%, n=259 in the reference. 'Nearly double' for 1.82x and 'nearly one in three' for 31.7% are fair characterizations. The pull-stat isolates the single most important figure. Rank context ('#1 of 307 nameplates') accompanies every headline number. No chart is needed; the comparison structure (drug vs alcohol leaderboards) does the visual work in prose.

ethics_reviewer.notes: The central ethical risk, equating drug detection with impairment, is handled with unusual care: the piece defines drug-positive as detection in the third paragraph, cites NHTSA's own null finding on THC crash risk, and carries a disclaimer stating the prescription-medication interpretation is inference, not a toxicology finding. The elderly-driver framing is sympathetic rather than stigmatizing and converts into actionable health advice (medication review). No individual is defamed; brand-level claims are factual and concern discontinued models.

general_editor.notes: Headline is a strong surprise-reversal with a specific, verifiable claim. Lede opens on the toxicology data without throat-clearing. Structure flows cleanly: ranking -> alcohol/drug divergence -> definition/measurement caveats -> demographic explanation -> full-strength counterargument -> actionable close. Pull-stat placement is clean. The counterargument paragraph is the strongest section and earns its position late, after the reader is invested. No structural revision needed.

legal_accuracy.notes: All quantitative claims are sourced and qualified. 'Drug-positive' is defined as detection, never asserted as impairment. The title's colloquial 'druggiest' is immediately defined in body text and the disclaimer, mitigating misreading. No claims about living individuals; Buick brand claims concern discontinued models and cite NHTSA data. All four sources are linked. No defamation exposure identified.

research_rigor.notes: Novel original computation: FARS 2014-2023 toxicology, 307 nameplates, n>=150 filter, Pearson r=0.504 between alcohol and drug rates. Four primary sources, all linked and quoted accurately (OR 1.25 unadjusted / 1.05 demographic / 1.0 with alcohol from the NHTSA crash-risk study; 39.9%->55.0% from Chihuri & Li 2026). Limitations are stated at full strength in research notes and the disclaimer: fatal crashes only, no drug-type breakdown, state testing-rate variation, 2018 cap-change artifact blending both eras. The prescription inference is explicitly flagged as demographic inference. One research-note transcription slip (thesis OR line) was corrected before this panel.

social_shareability.notes: Headline is highly shareable: 'The Druggiest Drivers in America Drive a Buick' subverts every expectation and is immediately qualified in the lede. The 16.6% pull-stat is tweetable. 'Read that again' is a quotable beat. The medicine-cabinet-not-meth-labs framing gives readers a counter-intuitive takeaway worth repeating. OG tags and meta description are in place. Minor: the nuance-heavy third paragraph will lose some skim-readers, but the disclaimer and lede carry the core claim.

voice_coach.notes: Zero em dashes. Zero banned phrases. The-starters 7.9%, well under the 15% cap. Sentence rhythm gate passes (variance 376.5, short 13.8%, long 41.4%). Dale Impactor III voice is fully present: 'Different leaderboard, different story.', 'The drivers did not change; the spreadsheet did.', 'Read that again.', 'a census of medicine cabinets, not a recklessness ranking.' Sardonic statistical persona sustained throughout with no AI tells. 500 words, exactly on target.

verdict: PASS round 0. All critics >= 8.5. No revision rounds needed.
